results.content:
and what it means — and every weight-level edit we tried either did nothing or broke the model. The same model fixes about a third of those errors when it is simply told which phrase to keep. [...] TL;DR. The Weight-Space Programming post fixed a small model’s maths by deleting a single direction from its weights, and reported that the same move did nothing for a different small model whose errors were “ordinary”. We tried the idea on two of our own models: a 4B English→Hindi translator and a 270M children’s-story writer. The boundary the post describes holds, cleanly. In the story writer, repetition is carried by one direction in layer 8; pushing away from it cuts repeated sentences from 32% to 2% and loops from 9% to 0%, and a control direction built the same way from shuffled labels makes repetition worse. In the translator, the meaning errors are not a habit but missing per-sentence information — which phrase matters here and what it means — and every weight-level edit we tried [...] We built one from 400 training sentences: the residual difference between the normal prompt and the same prompt plus “translate every detail, keep every qualifier”. At the divergence token it flips 15–31 of 86 errors at a small cost on correct output (+0.03 to +0.10 nats/token), where a random direction of the same size flips as many but costs +4 to +10 nats. That looked like a lead.

End to end it was a disaster. Applied at every position — the form a weight edit takes — and judged on full translations:

results.title: LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop — Latent Space
results.content: GPT-6 Astra Edits Qwen Weights: MATH-500 7.9% to 48.1% (Activity: 507): The linked discussion concerns MIT CSAIL’s Sparks of Weight-Space Programming work, with commenters pointing to the primary source rather than the summary site: rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming. The headline result is a direct weight edit of Qwen3.5-0.8B reportedly changing `131,072` weights (`~0.016%`) and raising MATH-500 accuracy from `7.9%` to `48.1%`, but the described mechanism appears to primarily suppress a pathological reasoning-loop attractor, reducing token-limit failures from `93%` to `33%`, rather than adding general mathematical competence. Commenters also note that the same intervention reportedly failed on a model without the looping pathology, e.g. Gemma 3 270M, limiting the generality [...] gains up to `3×`. Commenters reacted with surprise and framed this as a possible third axis of progress beyond parameter/data scaling and inference-time scaling: “weight space learning”. Several comments speculated about recursive self-improvement and future hardware acceleration, but there was no substantive technical critique in the provided top comments. [...] Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (Activity: 478): Takehi et al. propose Weight-Space Programming: frontier LLMs inspect and edit neural-network weight tensors from natural-language goals, without gradient descent/training loops. results.title: Weight-space programming - Wikipedia
results.content:
Weight-space programming is an approach in machine learning in which a general-purpose large language model (LLM) reads, interprets and directly writes the weights of another artificial neural network, without using gradient descent or a training loop. The term was introduced in November 2026 by researchers at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, who used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to identify what small networks had been trained to do from their weights alone, to write working networks from scratch, and to edit the Qwen3.5-0.8B language model.

## Background

[edit] [...] In the most widely reported experiment, Astra found the source of repetitive reasoning loops in Qwen3.5-0.8B and changed 0.016% of its weights, raising its score on the MATH-500 benchmark from 7.9% to 48.1% and on GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The same procedure produced no meaningful gain on Gemma "Gemma (language model)") 3 270M, leading the authors to conclude that editing "could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked."

On the same day, researcher Chandan Singh reported that Claude "Claude (language model)"), working as a coding agent, hand-wrote small transformers that solved ten algorithmic tasks such as addition and sorting, though some results were affected by weaknesses in the evaluation.

## Reception

[edit] [...] The authors described the results as "very early" and suggested they could matter for both optimization and interpretability. Commentators noted that most experiments used networks with only thousands of weights and that the work had not been independently replicated. Software engineer Sean Goedecke argued that a skilled researcher could have performed the same tasks, describing the Qwen fix as something "a competent human researcher could have and would have done", and compared editing weights directly to patching a compiled binary. spaCy creator Matthew Honnibal called the post's framing misleading, writing that the setting in which the model worked only from raw weights, without tools or running the network, was used only on networks of about 17,000 to 172,000 weights, while every

results.title: Weight-Space Programming: How LLMs Edit Network Weights | DataCamp
results.content:
IFEval

21.0% → 62.3%

Instruction following

The share of answers hitting the token limit fell to 33.1%, and because loops are not specific to math, instruction following improved too. Budget mattered: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away. Hugging Face's Ahsen Khaliq rebuilt the edited checkpoint from the logs and re-ran MATH-500 with the same settings, getting 51.0%.

## Where Weight-Space Programming Falls Short

Weight-space programming falls short wherever the problem is not a single, localized fault in the weights. The authors report two clear failures, and both are informative.
